The miner re-reads the profile at startup, so unplugging and restarting the service is enough to switch.

The default is L3 cache / 2 MiB, capped at the logical CPU count. On a 2 vCPU VPS with 54 MB of L3 that is two threads, which is also the best measured value: 814 H/s with two, 408 H/s with one. zmrig --autotune=8 # no pool required, 8 s per candidate threads hashrate verdict 1 499.625 H/s best so far 2 999.750 H/s best so far best: 2 thread(s) at 999.750 H/s autotune-best-threads=2 A difference under 2 % counts as noise, so it does not change the thread count because of one lucky run.

sudo zmrig -c /etc/zmrig/config.json --check config ok pool wss://my-relay.example.com:443/pool user=4Ad... algo=auto route connect 10.0.0.7:443, Host: my-relay.example.com proxy socks5 127.0.0.1:1080 threads 2 (default would be 2) mode auto, huge pages on, jit on --check reads the file and prints; it opens no socket and allocates no dataset. If the file is root-only, run it with sudo or you get cannot read …: check the path or run as root.

sudo systemctl stop zmrig sudo cp /etc/zmrig/config.json /etc/zmrig/config.json.bak sudo -e /etc/zmrig/config.json zmrig --check -c /etc/zmrig/config.json # parse and validate, do not mine sudo systemctl start zmrig --check exits non-zero and prints the offending key, which is faster than reading the journal after the service has already restarted four times. Autosave "autosave": true lets the miner rewrite the file when it changes something it owns (a tuned thread count, for example). If you want a file the miner never touches, set it to false and restart rather than editing a running config.

This tree ships three interchangeable mining engines behind one installer, one config file and one HTTP API: Engine Path Language Why it exists zmrig zmrig/ Zig the default: single binary, no runtime dependencies, same RandomX code xmrig src/ C++ the reference build, GPL-3.0, the widest algorithm and hardware coverage proxy proxy/ Node.js the farm front end; no hashing, only routing /etc/zmrig/engine records which one the installer chose, so every later oneclick.sh command acts on the same engine without being told again.

zmrig/src/ ├── main.zig startup, signals, the mining loop, report writing ├── options.zig the CLI surface, config-file parsing and validation ├── stratum.zig login, job parsing, share submission, refusals, cooldown ├── transport.zig TCP, TLS, WebSocket, SOCKS5/HTTP proxies, DNS ├── job.zig blob assembly, extranonce handling, target comparison ├── miner.zig thread pool, nonce spacing, hashrate windows, share accounting ├── api.zig JSON documents for the HTTP API ├── api_http.zig the HTTP server itself ├── report.zig ZMRIG1. report codes ├── health.zig the watchdog state machine ├── hugepages.zig reservation and verification of 2 MiB pages ├── topology.zig core detection, cache sharing, thread placement ├── autotune.zig picks thread count and affinity for the host ├── verify.zig share re-hashing for pool operators ├── log.zig the log format, levels and timestamps └── util.zig base64, hex, time, small helpers Nothing is linked beyond libc. There is no allocator in the hash loop, no background GC, and no dependency that could change behaviour between builds.

Parse flags, then config.json, then the engine marker — in that order, so a flag on the command line always wins. Detect the CPU: cores, SMT siblings, L3 size, NUMA nodes. Reserve huge pages; if the reservation fails, log the exact command that would fix it and continue rather than refusing to start. Build the RandomX cache (256 MiB) and, in fast mode, the dataset (2 GiB). This is the 15–25 s startup cost; light mode skips the dataset. Start the worker threads with the affinity chosen by autotune.zig. Open the stratum connection: DNS, transport, login, first job. Start the HTTP API (default 127.0.0.1:18080) and, if requested, the report file writer.

A job arrives as a 76-byte blob with a target. The miner writes the nonce into bytes 39–43, hashes, compares the result against the target, and on a hit sends submit upstream. Nothing on that path allocates, and nothing takes a lock: each thread owns a contiguous slice of the 32-bit nonce space, and its position is advanced by a stride chosen so two threads never collide. The scratchpad lives in huge pages for the whole run. That is the difference between 814 H/s and 634 H/s on the reference machine — see Benchmarks.

proxy/src/ is a small pipeline: server.js accepts rig connections, downstream.js models each rig, extranonce.js assigns prefixes, vardiff.js sets difficulty per rig, target.js compares hashes, upstream.js holds the single pool connection, tunnel.js handles WireGuard/Tailscale/ Cloudflare, and access.js enforces CIDR and token rules. blob.js is the only place that knows the layout of a Monero job — read that first.

pool/src/ accepts shares, re-hashes each one with zmrig --verify-share, keeps PPLNS weights as difficulty × time, and writes every block to audit.jsonl. Payouts go out through monero-wallet-rpc. pool/worker/ is a Cloudflare Worker that bridges WebSocket to TCP so the pool can run on a platform that only speaks HTTP.

Question File Why did a connection fail? zmrig/src/stratum.zig, zmrig/src/transport.zig Why this thread count? zmrig/src/autotune.zig, zmrig/src/topology.zig Why is hashrate low? zmrig/src/miner.zig, zmrig/src/hugepages.zig What does this API field mean? zmrig/src/api.zig Why did the service restart? zmrig/src/health.zig Why is a rig not being paid? pool/src/, then audit.jsonl Why is a rig not submitting? proxy/src/vardiff.js, proxy/src/target.js The longer C++ map — every directory in src/, the thread inventory and the RandomX pipeline — is in doc/ARCHITECTURE.md.
Every suite here runs without a real pool, and no suite needs a wallet.

./zmrig/out/zmrig --self-test # full: needs 2 GiB of RAM ./zmrig/out/zmrig --self-test=light # skips the dataset checks ./zmrig/tests/run.sh # self-test plus the API checks --self-test checks the reference rx/0 vectors, pipelined hashing, and that a dataset built from the cache produces the same result as a full-memory build. oneclick.sh verify calls it before it checks the fee.

zmrig/tests/health.sh runs the miner against a fake pool twice, to prove both directions: Case Expected A well-behaved pool health stays ok, nothing is logged as an error, no restart A pool rejecting every share health becomes rejected, the process exits code 3 so systemd restarts it, and the log says how to disable that Plus seven unit tests for the state machine (health.zig): a pause is not an error, one or two stale shares are normal, and a dip has to last before it counts as degraded.

It starts a fake pool, a TLS shim, HTTP and SOCKS5 proxies and a WebSocket server on the local machine, then makes the miner talk to all of them: ./zmrig/tests/net.sh --quick # 10 s per case ./zmrig/tests/net.sh # 18 s per case ./zmrig/tests/net.sh --soak # adds a 4-minute soak ./zmrig/tests/net.sh --only api,tcp Group Case What it proves Transport tcp, tls, ws, wss login, job, share submission ws path the server receives /miner wss via socks5 WebSocket over TLS through SOCKS5 CDN cloudflare wss on 443 with the right Host header Proxy http proxy, socks5 proxy CONNECT and auth reach the right target API http api, http api token, http api 404 summaries, token enforcement, unknown paths Failure login rejected, idle watchdog, pool failover the error is visible; reconnect and failover work hostile pool garbage input does not stop shares from being submitted Seed seed change four dataset rebuilds, mining continues Soak soak 4 minutes of seed changes, algorithm changes and a dropped link A full run takes 12–15 minutes on 2 vCPU, because each case has to produce a share and the suite runs in --mode light (50–70 H/s). A last run on that machine: 29 passed, 0 failed, 0 skipped Per-case logs land in /tmp/zmrig-net.XXXXXX/, printed at the end. When a case fails, read that case's log first (cloudflare.log, shim-cf.log, pool.log).

Ports. The suite uses 4800 for the pool and 4801–4813 for shims. A leftover process holding 4800 makes the cloudflare case fail with accepted=0 while the miner log says login ok. The script kills strays and refuses to start if something else owns the port. CPU load. Do not run benchmarks in parallel — you get either an OOM kill or a corrupted measurement. Huge pages. light mode means no 2 GiB reservation is needed; 50–70 H/s is expected, not a regression.

sudo ./oneclick.sh verify With the Zig engine it runs the self-test and then strings over the binary looking for known donation endpoints and addresses. With the C++ engine it runs scripts/verify-fee-free.sh, which additionally checks that the binary prints DONATE 0% when handed --donate-level=9. The check greps for endpoints and addresses, not for the word donate: the monitoring API legitimately returns "donate_level": 0, and a naive grep raises a false alarm. That has happened here, and it was fixed.

./zmrig/tests/cli.sh # flag parsing, help text, exit codes ./zmrig/tests/unit.sh # unit tests across the Zig modules node --test pool/tests/*.test.js bash tests/oneclick/plan.sh && bash tests/oneclick/config.sh && bash tests/oneclick/governor.sh plan.sh is the one that matters most after a change to the installer: it asserts the exact command a user would copy for a dozen flag combinations.

cd site && npm test # unit tests for the calculators and the command builder cd site && npm run build # fails on a broken internal link or a bad component The link check is the point of npm run build: onBrokenLinks and onBrokenMarkdownLinks are both set to throw, so a renamed page cannot ship as a 404.

The network suite uses its own ports and a fake pool, so it does not touch the real miner. But if the real miner holds the huge pages, the full --self-test may not have enough RAM for its dataset — use --self-test=light, or sudo ./oneclick.sh stop first.

documents.t: The point of this page is a decision: keep this machine, retire that one, and at what electricity price does either break even. It is not here to make the numbers look better. Paste one ZMRIG1. code per machine. Everything runs in this page — no code is sent anywhere. Machine codes Get one with sudo ./oneclick.sh report, or let the miner keep a file fresh with --report-file. Add machinesLoad sample dataExport JSONClear allImport JSON Assumptions Electricity price (per kWh)PSU efficiency (%)System overhead (W)XMR priceHashrate window10 s60 s15 minSession bestRevenue modelPer kH/s per day (pool rate)From network hashrateXMR per kH/s per day Every figure is an estimate. Network difficulty, coin price and share luck move constantly; the miner's own measurements are the only hard numbers here.

For each machine: hashrate H/s from the window you pick (10 s / 60 s / 15 min / best) power W wall = W_cpu / (PSU efficiency / 100) + system overhead energy kWh/day = W wall × 24 / 1000 cost $/day = kWh/day × price revenue XMR/day (one of two models, below) profit $/day = revenue × XMR price − cost efficiency H/W = hashrate / W wall Two revenue models, because they answer different questions: Per pool rate. You supply XMR per kH/s per day — the figure the pool shows on its dashboard. XMR/day = (hashrate / 1000) × xmr_per_khs_day This is the honest number for a switching pool such as MoneroOcean, because the algorithm switching is already inside the pool's rate. From network hashrate. Ignores switching, so use it to cross-check: blocks/day = (hashrate / network_hashrate) × 720 XMR/day = blocks/day × block_reward × (1 − pool_fee) The tail emission pays 0.6 XMR per block, 720 blocks a day.

The calculator adds a system overhead (25 W by default) and divides by PSU efficiency (87 %) because the number inside a report code is CPU package power: it excludes the mainboard, disks, fans and the losses of the PSU. Three levels of accuracy: A meter at the wall — the only exact one. Read the watts and either type them into the power column or pass --power W; a user value is used as-is and not scaled. RAPL / hwmon — zmrig --report reads it when the kernel exposes it. That is package power; add 15–30 W for the rest, which is what the two settings are for. Guessing from TDP — 30–50 % error is normal. Some machines will simply need the meter. The pwsrc field in a code says where the number came from. If it says none, type one.
documents.s: Why power has to be measured

documents.t: One 2 vCPU machine, 814 H/s, 45 W package, PSU 87 %, 25 W overhead, electricity at $0.10/kWh: W wall = 45 / 0.87 + 25 = 76.7 W energy = 76.7 × 24 / 1000 = 1.84 kWh/day cost = 1.84 × 0.10 = $0.184/day revenue = 0.814 × 0.000096 × $300 = $0.0234/day profit = 0.0234 − 0.184 = −$0.16/day That is the honest answer for a rented VPS at European electricity prices: mining Monero on a general-purpose CPU loses money. A machine you already own, whose power is free or nearly free, is a different calculation — and that is the case this software is built for. What the calculator cannot know Network difficulty, coin price and share luck move constantly. Everything here is an estimate built on your miner's measurements; the only hard numbers are the hashrate and, when --power is used, the watts.

A report code is how a machine describes itself without a server: one line of text, printable on a console, pasteable into chat, readable in a browser. sudo ./oneclick.sh report --power 45 ZMRIG1.eyJ2IjoxLCJpZCI6InZwc… # while mining: keep the file fresh zmrig --report-file /var/lib/zmrig/report.txt --report-interval 60 sudo cat /var/lib/zmrig/report.txt

ZMRIG1. followed by base64url of a compact JSON object. Version 1 of the format: { "v": 1, "id": "vps-sg-02", "ver": "6.32.1", "cpu": "AMD EPYC 7B13 64-Core Processor", "arch": "x86_64", "cores": 32, "thr": 2, "algo": "rx/0", "mode": "fast", "hs": [1461.2, 1470.5, 1466.1, 1478.9], "hp": [1168, 1168], "shares": [806, 0, 0], "hash": 881234012, "up": 86400, "pw": 22, "pwsrc": "rapl", "hw": 66.8, "health": "ok", "pool": "gulf.moneroocean.stream:10001", "ts": 1793412000 } Field Meaning hs hashrate over 10 s, 60 s, 15 min, session best (H/s) hp huge pages granted, needed shares accepted, rejected, failed hash total hashes computed up uptime in seconds pw, pwsrc watts, and the source: rapl, hwmon, user, none hw hashes per watt, when power is known, else null health the miner's view of its own income: ok, warming, degraded, stalled, rejected Nothing else is in it. No wallet address, no pool password, no public IP, no hostname beyond the worker name you chose yourself.

cut -d. -f2 report.txt | tr '_-' '/+' | base64 -d | python3 -m json.tool Or in a browser console: JSON.parse(atob("eyJ2Ijox…".replace(/-/g, "+").replace(/_/g, "/"))) You should not have to trust a decoder on a website to read a number your own machine produced. The calculator on this site decodes locally and sends nothing, but the two lines above are the whole trick.

--report measures a 10 s warm-up plus a window of --report-time seconds (15 by default), then reports the stable hashrate rather than the average since startup: an average would include the dataset build and come out 20–25 % low. In the calculator you pick the window: Window Use it for 10 s the current state of the machine 60 s the default; smooths brief dips 15 min a thermal-throttled or shared host session best what the machine can do when nothing else is running Comparing machines on different windows is the fastest way to draw a wrong conclusion about a CPU.

Give each machine a distinct --report-id. Let the miner keep writing its report file. Collect the lines and paste them into the calculator one per line — or as raw JSON, if you keep your own inventory. Codes survive copy-paste: the alphabet is base64url, so no line breaks, spaces or shell quoting are needed.

This repository contains both sides: the miner (zmrig, xmrig) and a Monero pool written in Node.js with no dependencies, under pool/. Running your own pool means the pool fee stays with you instead of going to a stranger — and your miners point at it exactly as they would at any other pool.

Item Value Pool fee 1.0 % of each block, taken before splitting, rounded down Hidden fees none Miner developer fee 0 % Payout threshold 0.01 XMR, plus the network fee The fee appears in the login reply the miner prints, in /api/config, and on the status page. Why 1 %: large Monero pools sit at 0.6–1 %, and this one does something most do not — it re-hashes every share with zmrig --verify-share before paying for it. That costs the operator real CPU, and it is the only thing that lets a miner know nobody is being paid for work they did not do.
documents.s: The 1 % fee, and what it buys

documents.t: # 1. a Monero node (testnet is fine while setting up) monerod --data-dir ~/.bitmonero --rpc-bind-ip 127.0.0.1 --confirm-external-bind # 2. the pool cd pool node src/index.js --check --config config.json # validate the config, then exit node src/index.js --config config.json # stratum + HTTP # 3. a miner, in another terminal zmrig -o 127.0.0.1:3333 -u 4YourMoneroAddress.rig1 -t 4 http://127.0.0.1:8080/ is the status page; curl -s 127.0.0.1:8080/api/stats returns the same numbers as JSON.

Node.js ≥ 18.17 — no npm install, no database. monerod with JSON-RPC reachable. zmrig in PATH so shares can be re-hashed. Without it the pool refuses shares rather than trusting them blindly: ./zmrig/build.sh --jobs 2 sudo install -m 0755 zmrig/out/zmrig /usr/local/bin/zmrig

A share is accepted only when the pool's own hash of the blob matches the hash the miner sent. A wrong hash is not merely rejected: the connection is closed. Share weight is difficulty × time, not share count — a slow machine is not punished and splitting one rig into three does not pay twice. Every block is written to audit.jsonl: reward, fee, each miner's payout, and the dust remainder listed on its own line instead of quietly folded into the fee. curl -s 127.0.0.1:8080/api/audit?limit=5 | python3 -m json.tool curl -s 127.0.0.1:8080/api/worker/4YourMoneroAddress

Where How Notes Render render.yaml (Docker) single port, WebSocket only; a free instance sleeps after 15 minutes idle Fly.io fly.toml + a 1 GB volume real TCP on 3333; monerod does not fit in 256 MB Cloudflare Workers pool/worker/ WebSocket ⇄ TCP bridge, no Durable Object needed Vercel static page only a function cannot hold a stratum connection fly launch --no-deploy --copy-config --dockerfile deploy/Dockerfile fly volumes create pool_data --size 1 fly secrets set DAEMON=https://node.example:18081 fly deploy Point a miner at it over WebSocket (requires the zmrig engine), or over TCP when the host exposes port 3333: zmrig -o wss://pool.example.com/stratum -u 4YourMoneroAddress.rig1 -t 4 zmrig -o pool.example.com:3333 -u 4YourMoneroAddress.rig1 -t 4

Keep state_file on a volume. Without it, a restart loses every miner's balance. /metrics exports Prometheus; /healthz returns 503 until a job template arrives from monerod. The audit log is append-only — rotate it with logrotate, never edit it. Change the fee wallet with OPERATOR_ADDRESS; the default lives in pool/src/operator.js. --check refuses configurations that cannot pay correctly: a fee outside 0–10 %, an unknown mode, a PPLNS window that is too short. Payouts via monero-wallet-rpc, the API and the security notes are in pool/README.md, and the deployment steps you must run yourself are in doc/SETUP.md.

Ten rigs in two buildings, one wallet, one connection to the pool. proxy/ does that: Node 18+, no dependencies, nothing to compile. sudo ./proxy/install.sh --user=4YourMoneroAddress --pool=gulf.moneroocean.stream:10001 Or without installing anything: node proxy/src/main.js start --user=4YourMoneroAddress --pool=gulf.moneroocean.stream:10001 install.sh --dry-run prints the systemd unit before writing it, and the banner prints the exact line each rig has to run.

Three ways a farm loses money, all with the same root: Duplicated work. A Monero nonce is 32 bits. Two rigs searching the same range means a share only gets paid once. The proxy gives each rig its own top nonce byte and keeps the bottom 24 bits for the rig — the same scheme as xmrig-proxy. The trap: prefix 0 is not a prefix. A blob with nonce 0 is the miner's signal to turn extranonce mode off, so handing a rig 0 silently puts it back into the shared range and earns less. One difficulty for every rig. A 500 H/s machine and a 20 kH/s machine on the same target produce one share an hour and one a minute. The small rig starves while still using full power. The proxy assigns difficulty per rig, targeting about 15 seconds per share. A login storm. The pool sees one login per rig, and a pool behind Cloudflare — or any free-tier service — rate-limits logins and then bans the IP. One connection from the proxy covers the farm, while each rig still shows up as its own worker (--user=wallet.rig3). The proxy does not hash. It checks each share's target (a BigInt comparison, microseconds) and forwards it; the pool re-hashes. It cannot fake work, and this implementation does not try.

node proxy/src/main.js doctor --user=4YourMoneroAddress --pool=gulf.moneroocean.stream:10001 ok pool gulf.moneroocean.stream:10001 answered -- 168 ms ok job difficulty -- 60011.2 ok a 5 kH/s rig would find -- 0.30 shares/hour at this difficulty The last line is the calculation people skip: shares per hour is hashrate × 3600 / difficulty. 0.30 means one share every three hours — fine for a long-window PPLNS pool, fatal for one with a high payout threshold.

One file per machine — sharing a file is the WireGuard version of the duplicate-nonce bug. Why this is the default recommendation: stable addresses (a changed ISP address requires no rig edits), UDP handled in the kernel so no added latency, no third party, and only one UDP port (51820) opened on the router — the stratum port stays on localhost.

node proxy/src/main.js start --user=4YourMoneroAddress \ --pool=gulf.moneroocean.stream:10001 \ --tunnel=tailscale --tunnel-token=tskey-auth-… Three things to know before choosing it: Funnel only serves 443/8443/10000, TLS only, and its bandwidth is not enough to poll a dashboard every second (it is plenty for stratum, a few kB/s). The free Personal plan is non-commercial. If the rigs are in the same tailnet, skip Funnel entirely and point them at <host>.<tailnet>.ts.net:3333; nothing is exposed to the internet.

documents.t: A quick tunnel is not a production path. It is good for exactly one thing: proving in two minutes that the network works. Property Consequence for mining Random hostname every start every rig needs updating after every restart No uptime commitment a dropped tunnel stops every rig at once No access control anyone with the name can mine to your wallet One more hop added latency on every job notification A named tunnel with a token fixes the hostname and the access control, and it is the right choice when only 443 is allowed. Even then the proxy stays the only thing exposed, and the rigs never see the internet.

curl -s http://127.0.0.1:3334/status | python3 -m json.tool /status reports, per rig, the hashrate derived from accepted shares and the local difficulty it was given, plus XMR/day when the network difficulty is known: node proxy/src/main.js start --user=4YourMoneroAddress \ --pool=gulf.moneroocean.stream:10001 \ --network-difficulty=350000000000 --block-reward=0.6 The figure is measured, not inferred from a CPU name, and it is null rather than a guess when the network difficulty is unknown.

Every switch below maps to one flag. What you see is exactly what the installer receives — nothing is added later. Wallet address Not entered yet. Shown on the pool dashboard to tell machines apart. After the install sudo systemctl status zmrig --no-pager -l sudo journalctl -u zmrig -n 40 --no-pager sudo ./oneclick.sh report --power 0 Remove it again sudo ./oneclick.sh purge --dry-run sudo ./oneclick.sh purge The same command, with plan curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/NggKhaiz/ZMRIG/BETA/oneclick.sh \ | sudo bash -s -- plan --pool gulf.moneroocean.stream:10001 Resolves the pool, the engine, the profile, the huge pages and the thread search, prints all of it, and writes nothing. You choose The installer receives Wallet --wallet <address> Rig name --rig-id <name> Pool --pool <host:port> or --pool tls://<host:port> Backup pools --failover <host:port>,<host:port> Fixed engine --engine zmrig or --engine xmrig (absent = automatic) Fixed profile --profile free or --profile watt (absent = automatic) 443-only network --cloudflare --ws-path <path> Proxy --proxy <url> Pool name filtered here --connect-to <host:port> Host refuses MSR writes --no-msr Rented hash --nicehash Do not tune the host --no-tune No thread search --no-autotune Keep the config (no --force) Two rules are worth knowing because they change the command rather than just adding a flag: Asking for WebSocket or a proxy forces --engine zmrig. The C++ engine has no WebSocket client and no proxy support, so the alternative would be a config nothing can run. A TLS pool becomes part of the --pool value (tls://host:port), because that is the form oneclick.sh parses. The address you type is validated before the copy button unlocks: 95 characters for a standard Monero address, 106 for an integrated one, base58 alphabet only. A pool host is validated as host:port, and a full stratum+tcp://… URL pasted from a provider page is accepted. The proxy field wants the whole URL — socks5://host:port or http://user:pass@host:port — because that is what the miner parses. The dial address is host:port only; it replaces the resolved IP but keeps the pool's hostname in SNI and the Host header, which is the point: a name blocked by a local resolver still works if you know where it lives.

The preview button copies the same command with plan in place of install. plan resolves the pool, the engine, the profile, the huge-page strategy and the autotune plan, prints them, and stops. It writes nothing. Neither command contains your wallet's private anything: a public address is the only credential involved, and it is visible to the pool by design.

Both engines compile to the same hash loop: zmrig/capi binds the C++ RandomX implementation into the Zig binary, so the numbers are the same within noise. The difference is everything around the loop. xmrig (C++) zmrig (Zig) Algorithms all of them (34+) the RandomX family: rx/0, rx/2, rx/wow, rx/arq, rx/graft, rx/sfx, rx/yada, panthera Transports TCP, TLS TCP, TLS, ws, wss Proxy partial SOCKS5 HTTP CONNECT and SOCKS5, with auth and remote DNS Monitoring API yes, complete yes, read-only, XMRig-compatible shape Report code for the calculator no yes (--report) Health watchdog no yes, restarts when earnings stop Measured rx/0 1075 H/s 1008–1103 H/s, same host, same config Both are measured on the same 2 vCPU machine; the spread is the host, not the engine. Benchmarks has the method.

RandomX on a normal VPS: either. zmrig is smaller, has the transport options and prints a report code, so it is what the installer picks. A switching pool (MoneroOcean and clones): zmrig still works — it advertises the whole RandomX family and the pool moves the rig between coins. It cannot mine the non-RandomX algorithms those pools also pay for, so a pool that values breadth more than depth is better served by xmrig. The installer's auto setting chooses xmrig for a switching pool for this reason; zmrig remains the 0 %-fee option either way. Any other algorithm (cn/heavy, ghostrider, KawPow): xmrig. zmrig refuses at argument-parse time rather than starting and failing to connect. A network that only allows 443, or a proxy: zmrig. See Networks that only allow 443.

The engine is recorded in /etc/zmrig/engine, so later subcommands (status, logs, bench, …) use the same binary without repeating --engine. sudo ./oneclick.sh install --wallet 4YourMoneroAddress --engine zmrig --force sudo ./oneclick.sh install --wallet 4YourMoneroAddress --engine xmrig --force Both binaries can stay installed side by side; the service runs whichever the marker names.
oneclick.sh [subcommand] [options] The default subcommand is install when a wallet is given and status when it is not.

Path What /usr/local/bin/zmrig the Zig miner /usr/local/bin/xmrig the C++ miner, when that engine is selected /usr/local/bin/zmrig-tune host tuning (--status, --hugepages 1G, …) /usr/local/bin/zmrig-bench reproducible hashrate measurement /usr/local/bin/zmrig-verify the zero-fee audit /etc/zmrig/config.json configuration, mode 600 /var/lib/zmrig/ state and the report file zmrig.service the miner: Restart=always, RestartSec=5, Nice=-10, LimitMEMLOCK=infinity, PrivateTmp=true zmrig-tune.service oneshot tuner, runs before the miner at boot http://127.0.0.1:18080/1/summary read-only monitoring API

Up to installer 1.2 the tool installed itself as xmrig-ocean. A new install does not silently leave the old one behind: /etc/xmrig-ocean/config.json is copied to /etc/zmrig/config.json (mode 600) if the new path does not exist yet. /var/lib/xmrig-ocean is moved to /var/lib/zmrig. The old unit is stopped, disabled and removed, so the machine does not end up running two miners after a reboot. purge removes both name sets, so an upgrade does not leave orphan files.

ALPHA ──► BETA ──► master newest default upstream history Every command in these pages uses BETA. To try ALPHA once: MINER_BRANCH=ALPHA sudo -E ./oneclick.sh install --wallet 4YourMoneroAddress sudo ./oneclick.sh update # back to the default branch update fetches the configured branch before checking it out, and stops with the branch name if it does not exist. That used to fail quietly.

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/NggKhaiz/ZMRIG/BETA/oneclick.sh \ | sudo bash -s -- --wallet 4YourMoneroAddress If the repository is already cloned: sudo ./oneclick.sh --wallet 4YourMoneroAddress That is the whole install. It installs the build dependencies, compiles the hash engine and the miner, measures the machine to pick a thread count, tunes the host, writes /etc/zmrig/config.json, creates zmrig.service, runs a self-check, and prints the hashrate it measured. Re-running is safe: no duplicate services, no overwritten config without --force, no rebuild when the binary is newer than the sources.

Decision How the installer chooses Engine zmrig (0 % fee). It advertises the whole RandomX family, so a switching pool can still move the rig to whichever coin pays best. --algo outside RandomX, or --engine=xmrig, selects the C++ engine. Profile free (maximum hashrate) everywhere, except a laptop on battery → watt (maximum hashes per watt). Threads Measured after the build: each candidate runs 8 s on the real dataset, the winner is written to the config. Huge pages Sized from the dataset. If the kernel grants fewer, it falls back to transparent huge pages and says so. Governor performance for free, the existing powersave governor for watt. See the same list without touching the machine: ./oneclick.sh plan ==> plan engine zmrig (RandomX family, 0% fee) pool gulf.moneroocean.stream:10001 algo auto (RandomX family: rx/0, rx/wow, rx/arq, …) profile free (auto: no battery, electricity is treated as free) mode auto (fast when RAM allows) huge pages none yet, the installer reserves what the dataset needs autotune 8 s per candidate, winner written to config.json service zmrig.service (systemd)

sudo ./oneclick.sh status # service, hashrate 10s/60s/15m, shares, huge pages sudo ./oneclick.sh verify # prove the 0 % fee sudo ./oneclick.sh logs 50 # last 50 log lines ==> verifying zmrig OK PASS rx/0 reference vector OK PASS pipelined hashing OK PASS full-memory dataset matches the cache OK no donation endpoints or wallets: 0% developer fee OK verified status only reports measured numbers: a miner that started a moment ago says warming up instead of quoting the previous run, because the dataset takes 15–25 seconds to build.

# free electricity: café, school, an office machine — maximum hashrate sudo ./oneclick.sh install --wallet 4YourMoneroAddress --profile free # every watt costs money: laptop, metered VPS — maximum hashes per watt sudo ./oneclick.sh install --wallet 4YourMoneroAddress --profile watt free uses every logical CPU, --mode fast, huge pages and --priority 5. watt drops to one thread per physical core (SMT adds 5–15 % hashrate for 30–40 % more power), does not pin the CPU to its highest clock, and stops by itself when a laptop switches to battery.

sudo ./oneclick.sh update # git pull, rebuild, restart sudo ./oneclick.sh uninstall # stop, remove service and binary, keep the config sudo ./oneclick.sh purge --dry-run sudo ./oneclick.sh purge # remove everything the tool created purge prints every path it created with its size, requires the word purge to confirm, resets vm.nr_hugepages to 0, and never touches a file it did not make. --dry-run lists without deleting.

No huge pages. In a container or an OpenVZ VPS the kernel may refuse; the miner logs the shortfall and continues at roughly 78 % hashrate. Nothing to fix — ask the host for 2 MiB pages. Service restarts in a loop. Almost always a config the miner rejects. Run sudo journalctl -u zmrig -n 60 and look for the first line after the binary starts; the installer validates the config before writing it, so this usually means someone edited it. the miner rejected the generated config. The wallet contains a character that is not valid base58. Re-run with a clean address. The rest of the failure modes are in Troubleshooting.

ZMRIG is a complete Monero mining setup, not a collection of scripts: Part What it is What it costs Miner XMRig 6.26.0 with every line of donation code removed, plus a complete Zig miner on the same RandomX engine 0 %, and that claim is checkable Installer oneclick.sh: one flag, host tuning, systemd unit, self-check, purge free Proxy one pool connection for a farm: extranonce per rig, per-rig difficulty, tunnels free Pool self-hosted Monero pool: stratum over TCP and WebSocket, PPLNS, every share verified 1 % of each block, nothing else The miner works with any pool. The 1 % on the pool in this repository is what keeps the project running; the miner itself takes nothing either way, and there is no account, token or telemetry anywhere in it.

The fee is provable, so it is checked. sudo ./oneclick.sh verify greps the binary for the upstream donation endpoints and known wallets, then runs hash self-tests so that "it found nothing" cannot mean "it looked at the wrong file". See the zero-fee page. There are no flags to start. --wallet is the only required input. The installer reads the CPU, the RAM, the hypervisor and the battery, then picks the engine, the thread count, the huge-page strategy and the governor, and prints the reason for each choice before it acts. ./oneclick.sh plan shows every decision and changes nothing. A miner that is not earning should say so. A rig whose pool rejects every share looks perfectly healthy from outside. zmrig judges its own numbers once a second and exits so the supervisor restarts it — twenty seconds of lost hashrate instead of a night of zero.
documents.s: Three decisions that shape everything else

documents.t: Linux x86-64 (Debian/Ubuntu, RHEL/Fedora, Arch; the script detects the distro). macOS and Windows can build the C++ engine, but the installer targets Linux. 2 GB of free RAM for fast mode, or --mode light with about 300 MB. systemd if you want it as a service. root, for huge pages, MSR and the service. A network connection for the first build. Everything is compiled on the machine; no binary is downloaded from anywhere.

Two ways to get numbers out of the miner: HTTP API Report code Use when the machine is on your network or VPN, or a script needs it the machine is behind NAT, or you want a number in a spreadsheet Security binds 127.0.0.1, optional Bearer token opens no port; you copy the code yourself Data everything, updated every second a snapshot at the moment it was written Many machines one endpoint each paste several codes at once

Enabled by --http-port; the installer turns it on at 18080. curl -s 127.0.0.1:18080/1/summary curl -s 127.0.0.1:18080/2/summary | python3 -m json.tool Path Content /1/summary, /summary compact single-line JSON, XMRig shape /1/status connection state /2/summary, /2/status same data, pretty-printed /json_rpc same as /1/summary, for older clients zmrig ... --http-port 18080 --http-access-token "$TOKEN" curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" 127.0.0.1:18080/1/summary A missing token returns 401 with JSON, an unknown path 404 with JSON, HEAD works for health checks, and every response carries Cache-Control: no-store. {"id":"zmrig","worker_id":"vps-sg-02","uptime":3600,"version":"6.32.1", "kind":"miner","ua":"zmrig/6.32.1","algo":"rx/0","paused":false, "donate_level":0, "connection":{"pool":"wss://relay.example.com:443","uptime":3600,"failures":0,"tls":true}, "hashrate":{"total":[814.2,810.5,805.1],"highest":902.7}, "hugepages":[1168,1168],"cpu":{"threads":2}, "results":{"shares_good":42,"shares_total":42,"hashes_total":2931842,"error_log":[]}} The API is read-only: there is no endpoint that changes a wallet or restarts anything. Even so, do not bind it to 0.0.0.0 without a token and a firewall — it reveals the worker name, the pool and your address.

That is a different question from "is the service active", and it is where money disappears quietly: a pool that rejects every share leaves a miner that is running, connected, printing hashrate, and earning nothing. The miner judges itself once a second and reports one of five states: State Meaning What happens warming building the dataset, or paused nothing (pausing is a feature) ok hashrate near this session's best, shares accepted nothing degraded below 80 % of the 10-minute peak (heat, a noisy neighbour) warning stalled the process is alive but not hashing error rejected shares were sent and none were accepted error sudo ./oneclick.sh status # hashrate: 1042.6 H/s (10s/60s/15m) # shares: 184/0/0 accepted # health: ok stalled or rejected for 15 minutes makes the process exit with code 3, and Restart=always turns that into a clean start. The trade is explicit: 16–30 seconds of lost hashrate instead of hours of earning zero. zmrig ... --no-health-restart # never exit on its own zmrig ... --health-restart=1800 # wait longer before giving up (seconds) zmrig ... --health-warmup=300 # ignore the first 5 minutes The state is also in the health field of a report code, so a fleet table can show the machines that are running and earning nothing.
documents.s: Health: still running, or still earning?

documents.t: One measurement, one line: $ sudo ./oneclick.sh report --power 45 ZMRIG1.eyJ2IjoxLCJpZCI6InZwc… # about 380–520 characters It takes 25–30 seconds: 15–20 s to build the dataset, 10 s of warm-up, 15 s of measurement, then a power sample. oneclick.sh report stops the service first — the running miner holds the huge pages, and a second dataset does not fit. Field Meaning id, cpu, cores, thr machine name, CPU model, physical cores, mining threads algo, mode algorithm, auto/fast/light hs[0..3] hashrate over 10 s, 60 s, 15 min, session best hp huge pages granted / needed shares, hash, up accepted, rejected, failed; total hashes; uptime in seconds pw, pwsrc watts and where they came from: rapl/hwmon (CPU package), user (wall meter), none pool, ts, ver pool, timestamp, miner version A code contains no wallet address, no pool token, no public IP. It is base64url-encoded JSON and you can read it yourself: cut -d. -f2 report.txt | tr '_-' '/+' | base64 -d | python3 -m json.tool While mining, let the miner keep the file fresh: --report-file /var/lib/zmrig/report.txt --report-interval 60 The installer enables that for the zmrig engine, so a later sudo cat /var/lib/zmrig/report.txt is enough.

Give each machine its own --report-id (or --rig-id). Let the miner write its report file. Paste the codes into the profitability calculator, one per line. The calculator totals hashrate, watts, kWh, power cost, revenue and profit, and exports JSON. There is no intermediate server. For 24/7 monitoring, scrape the API into Prometheus or Netdata over your own VPN; do not expose it to the internet.
documents.s: From one code to a fleet

documents.t: A "picky" VPS usually lands in one of four situations: Only outbound 443/tcp; 3333, 10001, 5555 are blocked. TLS required, plaintext stratum dropped, or DPI cutting unfamiliar packets. Everything must go through the organisation's proxy. Only certain address ranges are reachable (a CDN's anycast, an internal relay). The Zig engine handles all four. The C++ engine has no WebSocket client, so it cannot handle (1) and most of (2) — the installer switches engines rather than writing a config that cannot connect.

sudo ./oneclick.sh install --wallet 4YourMoneroAddress \ --pool my-relay.example.com \ --cloudflare=my-relay.example.com --ws-path /pool --cloudflare means: wss://<host>:443<path>, TLS on, engine zmrig. Forcing --engine xmrig alongside it is refused, not silently ignored. The same thing by hand: zmrig -o wss://my-relay.example.com:443/pool -u 4YourMoneroAddress -p x

documents.t: If the pool publishes a WebSocket endpoint on 443, no. If it does not, something has to bridge WebSocket to raw stratum. Two options that work: Relay When it fits Cost pool/worker/ in this repository the pool speaks plain TCP and you want a wss:// endpoint free Workers plan is enough for a farm Your own Worker you want to read every line of it free Workers plan The Worker in pool/worker/ is a byte pipe: it opens a TCP socket to the pool and pipes frames both ways. It does not see your wallet, and the pool sees the Worker's address, not your VPS. It does see the stratum traffic, which is why self-hosting matters if that concerns you. # 1. cd pool/worker && edit wrangler.toml, then: npx wrangler deploy # 2. point the miner at it sudo ./oneclick.sh install --wallet 4YourMoneroAddress \ --pool your-worker.workers.dev --cloudflare \ --ws-path /relay/YOUR_TOKEN --yes

# SOCKS5, no auth zmrig -o pool.example.com:3333 -u 4YourMoneroAddress --proxy socks5://127.0.0.1:1080 # HTTP CONNECT with credentials zmrig -o pool.example.com:3333 -u 4YourMoneroAddress \ --proxy http://user:pass@proxy.corp.example:3128 The Zig engine resolves the pool name through the proxy (remote DNS), so a poisoned local resolver does not matter.

Quad9 returns NXDOMAIN for gulf.moneroocean.stream; Cloudflare's malware resolver does the same for pool.supportxmr.com. A blocked name looks identical to a blocked port in a miner log. # keep the hostname for SNI and Host, dial a known-good address zmrig -o pool.example.com:3333 -u 4YourMoneroAddress \ --connect-to 203.0.113.10:3333 # or pin the CA of your own relay zmrig -o wss://relay.example.com/pool -u 4YourMoneroAddress \ --tls-ca /etc/zmrig/tls-ca.pem The installer copies a CA you supply to /etc/zmrig/tls-ca.pem: the unit runs with PrivateTmp=true, so a file in /tmp can disappear on restart.

documents.t: Retry a wrong wallet every five seconds. A rejected wallet is identified, that pool is left alone for 30 minutes, and the log says what to fix. Reconnect immediately after your IP is banned. Fifteen minutes per pool (--ban-cooldown), then the next pool in the failover list. Keep submitting after three shares were called invalid — a ten-minute pause instead of the hour-long ban xmrpool.eu hands out. Let twenty rebooting rigs reconnect in the same millisecond. Every retry is jittered ±20 %. These are the behaviours that separate one bad evening from a permanent block. More on pool choice in Pools.

documents.t: RandomX is a memory-bound proof of work: the hash loop reads a 2 GiB dataset in a random order. Almost everything that matters follows from that one sentence.

Huge pages. The largest and most obvious gain. A 4 KiB page size makes the dataset walk a TLB miss every few accesses. echo 1234 | sudo tee /proc/sys/vm/nr_hugepages # ~2.4 GiB of 2 MiB pages grep HugePages_ /proc/meminfo The installer does this and sets LimitMEMLOCK=infinity in the unit. To check the miner got them: the startup log prints huge pages 2336 MB, and the API reports "hugepages": [1168, 1168] (granted / needed). Measuring without huge pages Once 1234 pages are reserved, only about 1.2 GB of ordinary RAM is left. Running --no-huge-pages then gets the process OOM-killed (exit 137), because a second 2 GiB dataset does not fit. Set nr_hugepages to 0 before measuring that case, and remember to put it back. Fast or light mode. fast builds one 2 GiB dataset shared by every thread. light keeps a 256 MiB cache and rebuilds the dataset per hash: 76 H/s against 814 H/s on the same machine. Light mode exists for a VPS that cannot give 2 GiB, not as a power-saving option. Threads. One per physical core, two per core only when SMT helps: on the test host, two threads on two vCPUs gave 814 H/s and one thread gave 408 H/s, which is linear. SMT usually adds 5–15 % hashrate for 30–40 % more power, which is why the watt profile drops it.

Scratchpad prefetch mode (0/1/2/3): 823, 814, 823, 814 H/s — inside noise. The default (1) stays. Affinity on a 2 vCPU machine: identical. It matters on a many-core box with an uneven L3, which is a different measurement. Anything advertised as a large speed-up that is not huge pages, dataset mode or thread count should be measured before it is believed.

2 vCPU Xeon at 2.60 GHz, 3.9 GiB RAM, 1234 × 2 MiB huge pages, algorithm rx/0, one run per configuration. Configuration Hashrate Ratio default: 2 threads, huge pages, prefetch 1 814 H/s 100 % --no-huge-pages 634 H/s 78 % --mode light 76 H/s 9 % -t 1 408 H/s 50 % --scratchpad-prefetch=0 823 H/s 101 % (noise) --scratchpad-prefetch=2 823 H/s 101 % (noise) --no-affinity 814 H/s 100 % (noise) The same binary on the same host in a quieter session measured 1008–1103 H/s. That 20–25 % spread is why absolute numbers in documentation are close to useless, and why the ratios above are the useful part. C++ engine on the same host, for reference: 1075.7 H/s. The gap to the Zig engine is smaller than the gap between two runs.

zmrig --bench=20000 # fixed seed, fixed blob, dataset build excluded zmrig --report --power 45 # 10 s warm-up + 15 s window, prints a code sudo ./oneclick.sh bench # stops the service first, then measures Rules that make a measurement mean something: Stop the miner first. A running miner holds the huge pages; the benchmark then allocates in ordinary memory and reports about 20 % low. Measure the machine you care about. Absolute hashrate is a property of the host, not of the binary. Run each configuration twice. Under 2 % is noise. The full table, with the dates and the caveats, is in Benchmarks.

Symptom Usual cause What to do dataset ready takes 20–30 s normal: building 2 GiB not a fault; --mode light takes 0.6 s but keeps 9 % of the hashrate 20–30 % below expected hashrate huge pages were not granted grep HugePages /proc/meminfo; the log must say huge pages 2336 MB the process is killed, exit 137 out of RAM while building the dataset (huge pages already hold the rest) fix the huge-page reservation, or use --mode light cannot read …: check the path or run as root the config is root-only run with sudo config ok but nothing mines no -c, or no pool given --check only inspects the file it was given login failed: … repeats wrong wallet or pool, banned IP, wrong TLS mode read the line after it; try --transport tcp to rule TLS out connection lost repeatedly a CDN or NAT dropping a silent socket --keepalive-interval 60, --idle-timeout 120 share rejected: … stale job or difficulty, or the machine clock drifting check timedatectl; read the pool's own message API returns 401 an access token is configured send Authorization: Bearer TOKEN API unreachable from another machine it binds 127.0.0.1 by design do not expose it; use an SSH tunnel --tls-ca has no effect the file is in /tmp and the unit uses PrivateTmp put it at /etc/zmrig/tls-ca.pem

--background was ignored and the miner stayed in the foreground. It now forks, calls setsid and closes stdio. Reconnects were slow and then a storm. It waited the full --retry-pause after every drop and reset its counter on pool rotation, so a dead pool was hammered. Now: reconnect immediately after a session that had logged in, then 200 ms → 500 ms → 1 s → --retry-pause, with a counter that does not reset. Log files contained ANSI colour escapes. Files are plain text; stdout keeps colour. Command-line flags used to overwrite config values with defaults. zmrig -c config.json --verbose reset mode, huge-pages, retries. Only flags you actually type override now. report.enabled in the config started --report (measure, print, exit) instead of only writing the report file. The two are separate now. --tls used to imply "do not verify the certificate". It only selects the transport; verification stays on. One very long line from a pool killed the session. The line is dropped and warned about once when the session ends. --http-port never reached the config. Fixed; the installer writes the enabled boolean correctly. Ctrl-C hung while waiting for a login. The monitor closes the socket so the main thread can exit. A client that opened the API socket and went silent blocked the API thread. Every connection now has a 5-second timeout.
documents.s: Bugs that were fixed, so you do not have to meet them

documents.t: Is --mode light usable on a 1 GB VPS? It runs, at about 9 % of the hashrate (76 H/s against 814 H/s). Fine for keeping a connection or testing a config; for real mining, pick a VPS with at least 2.5 GB. How many threads? L3 cache / 2 MiB is right most of the time. If the VPS is throttled, drop one thread and measure again. Should a local pool use TLS? On the same machine or a private network, TLS costs CPU and adds no real security. Use it over the internet or through a CDN. Can it mine to several pools at once? Yes: several -o flags, or several entries in pools[]. It tries them in order and fails over after --retries failures. Does the API slow the miner down? No. It reads atomics that are updated once a second and never locks a worker. How long until the first share? Depends on pool difficulty: seconds on a test pool, minutes to hours on a real one with a small machine. A slow share is not a fault — check the hashrate and look for pool has been silent. How do I know the miner is mining to the right wallet? zmrig --check prints user=…, the API returns connection.pool, and the startup log prints wallet: …. Compare with the dashboard of the pool.

zmrig --version sudo ./oneclick.sh status sudo ./oneclick.sh logs 80 sed 's/"user": *"[^"]*"/"user": "REDACTED"/' /etc/zmrig/config.json Redact the wallet and any token before pasting. The log alone usually shows whether the failure is transport, TLS or the pool itself.

Two costs never show up on a hashrate chart: a pool paying less than it advertises, and an IP that can no longer connect. The first is a few percent; the second is 100 % of the income. Pool Fee Minimum payout Endpoint TLS on 443 Why MoneroOceanswitching 0 % 0.003 XMR gulf.moneroocean.stream:10001 gulf.moneroocean.stream:443 Pays the most per hash: the pool moves the rig to whichever RandomX coin is paying best and settles in XMR. Needs --algo=auto, which is the default. SupportXMR 0.6 % 0.1 XMR pool.supportxmr.com:3333 pool.supportxmr.com:443 The largest pool, so blocks are found often and the daily number moves less. Pick it when you want a steady figure rather than the maximum. C3Pool 0 % 0.003 XMR c3pool.com:3333 no Zero fee and a low minimum like MoneroOcean, without algorithm switching. The best failover pool because the infrastructure is completely different. HeroMiners 0.9 % 0.01 XMR monero.herominers.com:10191 no The lowest minimum (0.01 XMR) among the fee-charging pools. Fine for a small rig, but 0.9 % comes out of the payout. xmrpool.eu 0.9 % 0.07 XMR xmrpool.eu:3333 xmrpool.eu:443 Has its own TLS port on 443 for filtered networks, but the strictest ban policy of the group: three bad shares means ten minutes, then an hour. zmrig stops before that line. P2Pool mini 0 % 0.0004 XMR pool.xmr.pub:3333 no No pool owner and no fee; pays out with every block found. The most frequent payouts and the most variance. P2Pool nano 0 % 0.0004 XMR pool.xmr.pub:3334 no The even lighter P2Pool sidechain: fits a 1 vCPU VPS, but fewer shares mean smaller, scarcer payouts. Fees and minimums checked October 2026. Short names work directly with the installer: --pool=moneroocean, supportxmr, c3pool, herominers, xmrpool, p2pool, p2pool-nano. To see exactly what the repository would use, without installing: ./oneclick.sh plan --pool=supportxmr --wallet 4YourMoneroAddress

MoneroOcean pays the most per hash on a CPU, because it moves the rig to whichever RandomX coin is paying best and settles in XMR. Independent measurements put the gap at 10-30 % against a single-algorithm pool, which is larger than every fee difference in the table. It needs --algo=auto, which is the default here. SupportXMR is the low-variance choice. The largest pool finds blocks often, so the daily number moves less. Pick it when a steady figure matters more than the maximum, or as the backup behind MoneroOcean. C3Pool is 0 % with a 0.003 XMR minimum — the same shape as MoneroOcean without algorithm switching, on completely different infrastructure. The best second backup. Fees and minimums were read from the pools' own pages in October 2026. Fees change; ports and ban policies change less.

A pool bans an IP for three reasons, and all three used to be invisible: Cause A naive miner This one Wrong wallet, wrong port, TLS in the wrong place retries every 5 s, forever, from the same IP identifies the refusal, skips that pool for 30 minutes, prints the fix your IP is banned reconnects at once and extends the ban 15 minutes per pool, then the next one An overclocked rig producing bad shares keeps submitting, earns a 10-minute ban, then an hour after three invalid shares, stops for 10 minutes and says why Twenty rigs rebooting at once identical timestamps, login flood every retry jittered ±20 % Cooldowns are per pool: a pool that refused your wallet does not block the backup. --ban-cooldown=<seconds> changes the default of 900; the wrong-wallet case is floored at 30 minutes, because waiting five seconds does not fix a typo.

Rigs lose their connection to DNS filtering more often than to a ban. Documented cases: Quad9 returns NXDOMAIN for gulf.moneroocean.stream, Cloudflare's malware resolver does the same for pool.supportxmr.com, some ISPs block mining domains wholesale, and many VPS or corporate networks allow only 80 and 443. Four ways through, in the order worth trying: A backup pool on another domain. --failover=moneroocean,c3pool writes the extra pools into config.json; they are used only when the first cannot be reached or refuses this IP. A regional hostname — the same pool, a different DNS name. That only helps when the default alias is the filtered one. Port 443 with TLS, which looks like ordinary HTTPS: MoneroOcean gulf.moneroocean.stream:443, SupportXMR pool.supportxmr.com:443, xmrpool.eu xmrpool.eu:443. Use --pool=tls://host:443 so the miner knows that port expects TLS. --connect-to with an address resolved somewhere else. SNI and Host stay intact; only the dial address changes. dig +short gulf.moneroocean.stream # from a network that resolves it zmrig -o gulf.moneroocean.stream:10001 --connect-to 203.0.113.10:10001 -u 4YourMoneroAddress Option 4 is a workaround, not a solution: when the address changes, the connection breaks. Prefer 1–3. Details and the proxy recipes are in Networks that only allow 443.

documents.t: Country blocks. The client sees a refusal, not a reason. The cooldown stops it becoming a ban; it does not make that pool work. IPv6-only networks where the AAAA record is filtered — use --connect-to. Share rate limits (not login limits) on some pools. They arrive as rejects and the quarantine will stop the stream, but the right fix is fewer, larger shares via a higher target share time.

documents.t: Run one for a week, then the other, and compare xmrPerDay at the same hashrate: ./oneclick.sh install --pool=moneroocean --wallet 4YourMoneroAddress # a week later ./oneclick.sh install --pool=supportxmr --wallet 4YourMoneroAddress --failover=moneroocean --force MoneroOcean wins when the algorithm spread is real for your CPU (it changes with whichever coin is hot); SupportXMR wins when it is not, and always wins on steadiness. Measure, then decide — the answer changes from month to month.

# a full run: 20 000 hashes, including the dataset build ./zmrig/out/zmrig --bench=20000 # a quick check after a configuration change ./zmrig/out/zmrig --bench=15000 # the numbers for a dashboard (10 s warm-up + 15 s window) ./zmrig/out/zmrig --report --power 45 --bench uses the fixed seed 00112233…, a 76-byte blob and the lowest target, so every run hashes identical data and results are comparable. The dataset build (15–25 s) is outside the measured window. Rules that make a number mean something: Stop the miner before benchmarking. A running miner holds the huge pages; the bench then builds its dataset in ordinary memory and reports a figure that is too low. oneclick.sh bench stops and restarts the service to avoid this. Measure on the machine in question. Absolute hashrate depends on the host; do not compare to the table below. Run each configuration twice. Under 2 % is noise.

Configuration Hashrate vs default Comment Default: 2 threads, huge pages, prefetch 1 814 H/s 100 % baseline --no-huge-pages 634 H/s 78 % 22 % lost here, 36 % on another run --mode light 76 H/s 9 % only when RAM is short -t 1 408 H/s 50 % scales linearly --scratchpad-prefetch=0 823 H/s 101 % inside the noise --scratchpad-prefetch=2 823 H/s 101 % inside the noise --no-affinity 814 H/s 100 % 2 vCPU, no difference The same machine and binary in a quieter session: 1008–1103 H/s. That spread is the reason comparisons have to be relative. C++ engine on the same machine, same session: 1075.7 H/s — the gap to the Zig engine is within run-to-run variance, not a performance claim.
documents.s: A 2 vCPU VM (Xeon 2.6 GHz, 1234 huge pages of 2 MiB)

documents.t: The largest and least ambiguous effect. RandomX reads a 2 GiB dataset in a random pattern, and 4 KiB pages mean constant TLB misses. # reserve 1234 pages of 2 MiB (≈2.4 GiB) echo 1234 | sudo tee /proc/sys/vm/nr_hugepages grep HugePages_ /proc/meminfo The installer does this and writes it into the systemd unit (LimitMEMLOCK=infinity). To check the miner got them: startup logs huge pages 2336 MB, and the API reports "hugepages": [1168, 1168] (granted / needed). A practical warning: with 1234 pages reserved, ordinary RAM is down to about 1.2 GB. Running --no-huge-pages at that point gets OOM-killed (exit 137), because the 2 GiB dataset has nowhere to live. Lower nr_hugepages to 0 first.

fast builds one 2 GiB dataset shared by all threads → 814 H/s on this 2 vCPU machine. light keeps only the 256 MiB cache and recomputes the dataset per hash → 76 H/s. Nearly 11×. light is defensible when the VPS does not have the RAM, or to test a configuration quickly (0.6 s startup instead of 20 s).

Linear on this machine: 2 threads = 814 H/s, 1 thread = 408 H/s. There is no hidden sweet spot. On a throttled shared vCPU, extra threads can lower per-thread hashrate while still raising the total; measuring is the only way to know.

--scratchpad-prefetch 0/1/2/3: under 1.5 %, i.e. noise. Leave the default. --no-affinity on 2 vCPU: nothing. --no-optimized-init: affects dataset build time, not hashrate. Ignore advice to raise priority for hashrate: priority changes how the OS shares CPU, it does not make arithmetic faster. It helps when the machine does other work.
documents.s: Settings that made no measurable difference

documents.t: # 1. background state sudo ./oneclick.sh stop grep -E "HugePages_Total|HugePages_Free" /proc/meminfo # 2. measure the default ./zmrig/out/zmrig --bench=15000 # 3. variants, each twice ./zmrig/out/zmrig --bench=15000 -t 1 ./zmrig/out/zmrig --bench=15000 --no-huge-pages # only after lowering nr_hugepages ./zmrig/out/zmrig --bench=15000 --mode light # 4. keep the winner in the config, then start sudo ./oneclick.sh start Write the numbers down with the date and host name. Six months later you will want them.

Hashrate is not the whole story. A machine doing 814 H/s at 95 W beats one doing 900 H/s at 130 W. Measure at the wall, or read package power from RAPL: cat /sys/class/powercap/intel-rapl:0/energy_uj # twice, one second apart zmrig --report reads it for you and records the source in the report code (pwsrc: rapl, hwmon, user or none), along with hw — hashes per watt (the 60-second hashrate divided by power). That is the number --profile watt optimises, so the code carries it instead of leaving everyone to divide. hashrate power H/W --profile free the most the machine can do highest lower --profile watt a few percent lower (SMT threads dropped) 30–40 % lower on the SMT part higher Those rows describe a direction, not your machine: power cannot be measured inside this repository's container (RAPL is blocked), so the watt figures are inferred from P ∝ V²·f and published SMT data. The hashrate side is measured. On a machine with RAPL, run zmrig --report under both profiles and compare hw — then the conclusion is yours, at your electricity price. The profitability calculator turns those watts into money.

This build mines 100 % for the pool and wallet you configure. No developer fee, no time slicing, no second stratum session, no hidden wallet. The claim is worth nothing without a way to check it, so the checking comes first. ./scripts/verify-fee-free.sh # source + binary audit ./scripts/verify-fee-free.sh --source-only # no binary needed The script asserts six things: Both donation constants are 0. DonateStrategy is absent from the tree and from CMakeLists.txt. No wallet address and no donation hostname exist under src/. Network has no donation plumbing. The built binary contains no developer wallet and no donation endpoint. The binary reports DONATE 0% even when started with --donate-level=9. Manual equivalents: strings build/xmrig | grep -Ei 'donate\.|moneroocean\.stream|^[48][1-9A-HJ-NP-Za-km-z]{95}$' # -> nothing ./build/xmrig --dry-run --url pool.example.com:3333 --user TEST --donate-level=9 | grep DONATE # -> DONATE 0% (fee-free build) curl -s http://127.0.0.1:18080/2/summary | jq .miner.donate_level # -> 0 At runtime the log never prints dev donate started, and the HTTP API reports "donate_level": 0.

Upstream XMRig keeps the fee in src/net/strategies/DonateStrategy.cpp: Pools::donateLevel() returns donate-level (default 1, minimum 1), and Network runs a second strategy that, roughly every 100 minutes, pauses your pool for one minute and connects to a developer pool (m_idleTime = (100 - level) * 60 s, m_donateTime = level * 60 s). The donation pool receives the hashes. In the MoneroOcean-flavoured tree this fork descends from, that endpoint was xmrig.moneroocean.stream:10001/20001 with a hardcoded wallet, and the fee was silently disabled only when the first configured pool host contained moneroocean.stream — meaning everyone mining anywhere else paid it.

File Change src/donate.h kDefaultDonateLevel = 0, kMinimumDonateLevel = 0; no address in the tree src/net/strategies/DonateStrategy.{h,cpp} deleted CMakeLists.txt donation sources removed from the target src/net/Network.{h,cpp} m_donate removed; no second strategy, no donation submit path, no tick src/core/Miner.{h,cpp} setJob(job, donate) → setJob(job); job index always 0 src/base/net/stratum/Pools.{h,cpp} donateLevel() is a constexpr returning 0; the "disable fee if the pool matches" hack is gone src/base/kernel/config/BaseTransform.cpp --donate-level / --donate-over-proxy parsed and deliberately ignored src/core/config/Config_default.h "donate-level": 0 src/Summary.cpp prints DONATE 0% (fee-free build) --donate-level and --donate-over-proxy are still accepted so existing scripts, configs and dashboards keep working. Their values do nothing, and the miner logs that it is ignoring them instead of silently honouring a number it cannot pay.

A donation round on RandomX is not 1 % of the time: the developer pool has a different seed → a full 2 GiB dataset re-initialisation; every worker thread is stopped and restarted → VMs and JIT code rebuilt, 2 MiB scratchpads faulted in again; the nonce window resets and in-flight hashes are lost; two extra pool sessions per round (connect, login, job). Removing the fee therefore returns more than 1 % — typically 2–4 % of real hashrate on RandomX, plus the full time slice.

documents.t: The donation address in this project is documentation: a human may copy it, no code path reads it. It appears in doc/DONATE.md and nowhere under src/, zmrig/, pool/ or oneclick.sh — which is exactly what the audit checks. Sending something is an invitation accepted or ignored, never a charge.
documents.s: The published address is not a fee

documents.t: XMRig is GPL-3.0. Deleting the donation code is a permitted modification of source you received; copyright headers and the licence stay untouched. Upstream is funded by that 1 % donation; this fork takes nothing and publishes one optional address for people who insist.
The miner has no developer fee and will not get one. This page exists for the people who ask where to send something anyway. Nothing in the software reads the address below.

46SQLW7DXaq6GJaQbHUFMAhd1VYpfQFJQ2gfZo9TCB8bf9vnf1MUwAD2Fwj6KMsY4RU3oKA3x6hByg8BKg7FfMWn6ysb5tJ Monero (XMR) only. Anything else — BTC, ETH, USDT, wrapped tokens — is lost, and no one can recover it. A standard mainnet address, 95 characters, network byte 18. Not an integrated address, not a subaddress. The same wallet as the pool fee. pool/src/operator.js decodes to this exact address, and every pool instance publishes it at /api/config and on its status page. One wallet, one audit trail.

Do not trust a string because it is on GitHub. The address starts with 46SQLW7D and ends with n6ysb5tJ; a Monero address is base58 with a 4-byte Keccak-256 checksum, so a typo cannot survive a decode. from Crypto.Hash import keccak # pip install pycryptodome ALPHABET = "123456789ABCDEFGHJKLMNPQRSTUVWXYZabcdefghijkmnopqrstuvwxyz" ADDRESS = "46SQLW7DXaq6GJaQbHUFMAhd1VYpfQFJQ2gfZo9TCB8bf9vnf1MUwAD2Fwj6KMsY4RU3oKA3x6hByg8BKg7FfMWn6ysb5tJ" def decode_block(text, size): value = 0 for char in text: value = value * 58 + ALPHABET.index(char) return value.to_bytes(size, "big") raw = b"" for offset in range(0, len(ADDRESS), 11): group = ADDRESS[offset:offset + 11] raw += decode_block(group, 8) if len(group) == 11 else decode_block(group, 5) body, checksum = raw[:-4], raw[-4:] digest = keccak.new(digest_bits=256, data=body).digest()[:4] print(len(raw), body[0], "OK" if digest == checksum else "BAD") # 69 18 OK A bad checksum means a typo, a truncated copy, or something that was never a Monero address.

No effect on the miner. The address is absent from src/, zmrig/, pool/ and oneclick.sh, so sudo ./oneclick.sh verify reports a 0 % fee whether the address is published or not. No supporter edition. There is one binary and it mines at full speed for everybody. Anyone selling a "faster build" is not this project. No priority support, roadmap vote or badge. Issues are answered in the order they arrive and by how reproducible they are. No subscription. There is nothing recurring to cancel.
documents.s: What a donation does not buy

documents.t: Mine to the pool. The 1 % fee is what funds the work, and it only exists while somebody is mining. Send a measurement. zmrig/tests/ab.sh compares two settings on the same machine; a before/after table settles arguments that opinions do not. Report a bug with the command, the full output and the hardware. Light mode on a 2 GiB VPS and MSR reads on bare metal are where a report is worth the most. Send a patch. Pool share accounting, the Zig front end and doc/ typos are all fair game.
documents.s: What helps more than a transfer

documents.t: This project has published exactly one, the string above. Addresses in forks, issues, pull requests, videos, chat messages or "official mirror" sites are not ours. Compare against doc/DONATE.md in the repository history (git log -p doc/DONATE.md), not against a screenshot.

Donations are public on the Monero chain by design. Nothing else is collected: the miner sends no telemetry, the site has no analytics, and the pool keeps no account for a donor. To stay unlinked, send without a payment ID and from an address you have not used elsewhere.
